references.text: The parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus says exactly the same thing to a scribe who wants to follow him: 'Foxes have holes and birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.'

Daniel's vision of 'one like a son of man' coming with the clouds of heaven and receiving dominion and kingdom. Jesus uses the title 'Son of Man' for himself, which has its background in this prophecy.
Paul writes that Jesus Christ, though he was rich, became poor for your sake, so that by his poverty you might become rich. This reflects Jesus' earthly life without a fixed home.
The prophecy about the Lord's suffering servant who was despised and forsaken by men, a man of sorrows. Jesus' homeless life reflects the humble and suffering servant figure described by Isaiah.

The Christ hymn in Philippians describes how Jesus, being in the form of God, did not count equality with God something to be grasped but took the form of a servant. His lack of a place to lay his head illustrates this self-emptying.
The verse just before, where a man says to Jesus that he will follow him wherever he goes – this is the context for Jesus' answer about the Son of Man's homelessness and what it costs to follow him.
Already at Jesus' birth there was no room for them in the inn, which points forward to his later life without a fixed home.
Jesus says that a prophet is not without honor except in his hometown. This sheds light on the theme of Jesus' rejection and lack of a place to belong.

John writes that Jesus was in the world, and the world came into being through him, but the world did not know him. He came to what was his own, and his own people did not receive him. This underscores Jesus' foreignness in the world.

The witnesses of faith in the Old Testament who wandered about without a fixed home, dressed in skins, persecuted and suffering – the world was not worthy of them. Jesus' homelessness places him among God's faithful who suffered in the world.
